summary: Describes the standardization collaboration between 3GPP, the mobile phone standards group, and the IETF. It explains how the two organizations coordinate work where Internet protocols are used in mobile networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Two clubs that build things for the same playground agree how to work together so their pieces fit.

questions: how does the ietf work with 3gpp
what is a 3gpp liaison in the ietf
subtitle: How the mobile-standards group 3GPP and the IETF agreed to share drafts, talk to each other and avoid duplicating work.

tldr.problem: 3GPP wanted to build mobile systems on Internet protocols and needed a clear way to work with the IETF, which has its own rules and open processes.
tldr.mechanism: The two organizations agree on principles: each keeps its own rules, drafts are shared, people talk by mailing list, and a 3GPP rapporteur and an IAB-appointed 3GPP liaison act as contact points.
tldr.outcome: A non-protocol Informational document that sets the working relationship. It does not specify any Internet standard.

today: RFC 3113 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the collaboration as agreed in June 2001.

sections.title: Purpose of the Collaboration
sections.content:
RFC 3113 sets out principles and guidelines for collaboration between the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) and the IETF. The goal is timely development of technical specifications that allow maximum interoperability with existing fixed and mobile Internet systems, devices and protocols.

Each organization keeps operating under its own rules and procedures, including those for intellectual property rights, specification development, approval and maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: Both clubs keep their own rules, but they agree on a goal: things they build should work together.

sections.title: Why the Two Groups Work Together
sections.content:
3GPP has seen the benefit of adopting Internet specifications. Its preferred approach is to use Internet standards unchanged if feasible, and it has no intention of duplicating IETF work. If additions or changes are needed, 3GPP takes its concerns directly to the appropriate IETF working group, or to an Area Director if no working group fits.

The IETF gains access to 3GPP wireless expertise. The RFC lists 3GPP's Technical Specification Groups and their areas: TSG-RAN and TSG-GERAN for radio access networks, TSG CN for mobility management and core network protocols, TSG-T for terminals and applications, and TSG-SA for services and system aspects including architecture, security and operations and maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: One club knows a lot about phones and radios. The other knows the Internet. Each borrows the other's knowledge instead of reinventing it.

sections.title: Sharing Documents and Talking
sections.content:
Both organizations encourage sharing draft documents of mutual interest. 3GPP documents are on its public web site, and IETF documents, including Internet Drafts, are on the IETF site and shadow sites. Each side can learn how the other's document structures work by contacting the named contact points: 3GPP contact points for IETF people, and the IETF Area Directors for 3GPP people.

Informal communication at working level is encouraged whenever possible. Most technical discussion and decision making in both groups happens on mailing lists, and interested individuals are encouraged to subscribe and take part. Formal communication is also allowed when needed, and the relevant IETF Area Directors and 3GPP technical leadership are encouraged and authorized to facilitate it.
sections.plainLanguage: They swap their notebooks and mostly chat by email. If something needs a formal letter, the leaders can send one.

sections.title: Contact People and Participation
sections.content:
3GPP establishes an IETF rapporteur function in TSG-SA, which is the initial 3GPP contact point for the collaboration. On the IETF side, the preferred way to work is through working groups, but the RFC proposes that the IAB appoint a specific 3GPP liaison as an initial contact for administrative matters that cannot be handled otherwise. This liaison is not expected to attend 3GPP meetings, works by email and cannot make exceptions to IETF policies and procedures.

The IETF may, case by case, appoint a rapporteur to represent it at 3GPP technical meetings. IETF meetings are open to any interested individuals, and 3GPP partners or individual members may take part under existing IETF procedures. The RFC notes it is a non-protocol document and does not directly affect Internet security.
sections.plainLanguage: Each club names a go-to person, so anyone with a question knows who to ask.
